narrative:
The model estimated a 67.8% probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. In practical terms, it judged failure more likely than success, and that judgment led to denial of your law school application.

The denial was driven mainly by your LSAT score. It was the most influential factor and pushed the prediction toward bar failure. Your score of 23.50 is far below the average of 37.18 among students who were accepted, so the model treated it as a strong warning sign about bar readiness. The second most influential factor was your Year 3 class decile. At 2.00, you were well below the accepted-student average of 5.79, and this also pushed the prediction toward failure. The third factor was your undergraduate GPA. At 3.10 it is only slightly below the accepted average of 3.23, and among these three factors it was the one that pushed toward passing, but it was not enough to offset the LSAT and Year 3 decile.

To improve your position, focus first on retaking the LSAT after structured preparation and consider whether any circumstances affected your earlier score. Strengthen your academic record where possible, and ask admissions how they review applicants with a bar-readiness concern. A later application that shows clear improvement in the factors most tied to bar success would give you a stronger case.
